\chapter{Eye, Ear, Mouth, and Nose}
\label{ch:gu-face-parts}
\hlchaptermodality{18}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the eye, ear, mouth, and nose in Gujarati, tell a nasal that only marks a sound from one that marks the neuter gender, and say which two of the four are unbroken cousins of their English counterparts.}

The chapter closes on \gu{નાક}, completing the face: the reader produces \gu{આંખ}, \gu{કાન}, \gu{મોઢું} and \gu{નાક} with their genders (f, f, n, n), names \gu{આંખ} and \gu{નાક} as unbroken PIE cousins of eye and nose, states that \gu{મોઢું}'s nasalized -ũ is the same neuter tell carried by every -\gu{વું} verb infinitive while \gu{નાક} shows a neuter noun does not always carry it, and reaches back to \gu{વાંચવું}'s medial nasal and \gu{જવું}/\gu{જોવું}'s one-mark contrast.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āṅkh]{\gu{આંખ} — an eye, and a nasal that is not what it looks like}

\label{lesson:GU-C12-aankh}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{બહેન}} (\emph{bahen}) closed a chapter about people. This chapter checks on how someone is — starting with the parts of the body a friend might actually ask about.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{આંખ}} — \emph{āṅkh} — \textbf{eye}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{આ}} the independent long-\emph{ā}, then the nasal dot \textbf{\gu{ં}} sitting on top of it — exactly the medial anusvāra you first read inside \textbf{\gu{વાંચવું}}, doing the same job here, in the middle of a noun rather than a verb — then \textbf{\gu{ખ}}, the aspirated \emph{k}. \textbf{Note what this nasal is NOT}: it does not mark \textbf{\gu{આંખ}} as neuter — the word is feminine. A nasal dot in the middle of a word is a \textbf{sound}, present or absent as pronunciation happens to need it; it is a different thing entirely from the grammatical \emph{-ũ} ending you will meet again soon, and this chapter keeps the two apart on purpose.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{āṅkh} is inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit \emph{akkhi}, from Sanskrit \textbf{akṣi}, \textquotedblleft{}eye.\textquotedblright{} The root is Indo-European *\emph{h\textsubscript{3}ek\textsuperscript{w}-}, \textquotedblleft{}eye; to see,\textquotedblright{} and it survives unbroken in English \textbf{eye} itself, in Latin \emph{oculus} (behind \textbf{ocular}), and in Greek \emph{ósse}. This is \emph{bhāī}'s kind of cousin, not \emph{bahen}'s: a straight line back to the same ancestor, no borrowing and no detour.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{āṅkh} — eye
  \item \emph{Match:} the medial nasal here against the one in \textbf{\gu{વાંચવું}}
  \item \emph{State:} is this nasal a gender marker? (No.) Is \textbf{āṅkh} neuter? (No — feminine.)
  \item \emph{Trace it:} PIE \emph{h\textsubscript{3}ek\textsuperscript{w}-} $\to$ Sanskrit \emph{akṣi} $\to$ \textbf{\gu{આંખ}}, and $\to$ English \textbf{eye}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}eye.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Āṅkh}.) Which English word is the same word by unbroken descent? (\textbf{Eye}.) Does the nasal dot in \emph{āṅkh} mean the word is neuter? (\textbf{No} — \emph{āṅkh} is feminine; the dot is only a sound.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%86\%E0\%AA\%82\%E0\%AA\%96}{Wiktionary: \gu{આંખ}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%85\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%B7\%E0\%A4\%BF}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit akshi}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kān]{\gu{કાન} — an ear whose own root is unsettled}

\label{lesson:GU-C12-kaan}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{આંખ}} traced back cleanly to a confirmed Indo-European root. The next body part will not be nearly as tidy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{કાન}} — \emph{kān} — \textbf{ear}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ક}} \emph{ka}, \textbf{\gu{ા}} long-\emph{ā}, \textbf{\gu{ન}} \emph{na}. All three already yours.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a gender that changed on the way here}]
\textbf{\gu{કાન}} is feminine in Gujarati. Its Sanskrit ancestor, \textbf{karṇa}, was \textbf{masculine}. Nothing about inheriting a word guarantees its gender comes along unchanged — \textbf{\gu{મિત્ર}} kept Sanskrit's masculine, but \emph{kān} did not keep \emph{karṇa}'s. Gender, like the gender of \textbf{\gu{આંખ}} or \textbf{\gu{બહેન}}, has to be learned with each noun as it stands today, not projected backward from what its ancestor was — the same caution \textbf{\gu{રોટલી}}'s chapter drew from its own \textbf{-ī} ending.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{kān} is inherited from Old Gujarati \emph{kāna}, through Apabhramsa and Prakrit \emph{kaṇṇa}, from Sanskrit \textbf{karṇa}, \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} Past that point, no agreement exists. Proposed origins include a root for \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{defect}\textquotedblright{} (with \textquotedblleft{}ear\textquotedblright{} as a later, narrower sense), a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{point}\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{spike},\textquotedblright{} a root meaning \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{handle}\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{grip},\textquotedblright{} and a connection to \textbf{śṛṇoti}, \textquotedblleft{}to hear.\textquotedblright{} None of these has won out. \emph{Kān} joins \emph{roṭlī} as a second word in your Gujarati vocabulary whose Sanskrit form is certain and whose deeper root is not — the honest answer, said plainly rather than picked at random.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{kān} — ear, and \textbf{āṅkh} — eye
  \item \emph{State:} \emph{karṇa}'s Sanskrit gender against \emph{kān}'s Gujarati gender (masculine $\to$ feminine)
  \item \emph{Name:} two of the four disputed origins scholars have proposed for \emph{karṇa}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{āṅkh}'s confirmed PIE root against \emph{kān}'s unsettled one
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}ear.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Kān}.) Did its gender change between Sanskrit and Gujarati? (\textbf{Yes} — masculine to feminine.) Is \emph{karṇa}'s own root settled? (\textbf{No} — several proposals, no agreement.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%95\%E0\%AA\%BE\%E0\%AA\%A8}{Wiktionary: \gu{કાન}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%B0\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%A3}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit karna}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moḍhũ]{\gu{મોઢું} — the tell you have been hearing all along}

\label{lesson:GU-C12-modhu}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{કાન}} (\emph{kān})'s own gender shifted away from Sanskrit's. The next body part wears its gender in plain sight — the same nasalized ending you have heard on nearly every verb in this book.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{મોઢું}} — \emph{moḍhũ} — \textbf{mouth}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{મ}} \emph{ma}, \textbf{\gu{ો}} the \emph{o} sign, then a new letter: \textbf{\gu{ઢ}}, the retroflex aspirated \emph{ḍh} — curl the tongue back as for \textbf{\gu{ટ}} and \textbf{\gu{ણ}}, and add the puff of breath that made \textbf{\gu{ધ}} aspirated. Then \textbf{\gu{ું}}, \emph{u} with the nasal dot. \emph{Mo-ḍhũ}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the neuter tell, named plainly}]
Every verb infinitive in this book ends in the neuter \textbf{-\gu{વું}}: \emph{hovũ}, \emph{javũ}, \emph{jāṇvũ}, \emph{lakhvũ} — a whole word class marked by that one nasalized ending. \textbf{\gu{મોઢું}} shows the same ending doing the same job on a \textbf{noun}: \emph{moḍhũ} is \textbf{neuter}, and the nasalized \emph{-ũ} is the single most recognizable tell for it. Not every neuter noun wears it — \textbf{\gu{પાણી}} and later \emph{nāk} do not — but when you do see or hear a word end this way, neuter is the way to bet. And do not confuse it with \textbf{\gu{આંખ}}'s nasal: that one sat in the \textbf{middle} of a feminine word and marked nothing about gender at all. This one sits at the \textbf{end}, and it does.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{moḍhũ} is inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit \textbf{muha}, from Sanskrit \textbf{mukha}, \textquotedblleft{}mouth, face.\textquotedblright{} It has a formal doublet, \textbf{\gu{મુખ}} \emph{mukh}, borrowed directly from the same Sanskrit word the way \emph{kuṭumb} was — the everyday and the formal register, side by side, from one ancestor reached by two different roads. Past Sanskrit, \emph{mukha}'s own root is not agreed upon — a second open question, alongside \emph{karṇa}'s, rather than a guess dressed up as an answer.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{moḍhũ} — mouth
  \item \emph{State:} what gender the \emph{-ũ} ending marks, and one verb infinitive that wears the same ending
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{moḍhũ}'s end-of-word nasal against \emph{āṅkh}'s middle-of-word one
  \item \emph{Name:} \emph{moḍhũ}'s formal doublet, and how it reached Gujarati (borrowed whole, like \emph{kuṭumb})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}mouth.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Moḍhũ}.) What gender does its \emph{-ũ} ending mark? (\textbf{Neuter}.) Name the formal doublet of \emph{moḍhũ}. (\textbf{\gu{મુખ}}, \emph{mukh}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%AE\%E0\%AB\%8B\%E0\%AA\%82}{Wiktionary: \gu{મોં}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%96}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit mukha}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāk]{\gu{નાક} — the whole face, run back}

\label{lesson:GU-C12-naak}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{આંખ}}, \textbf{\gu{કાન}}, \textbf{\gu{મોઢું}} — eye, ear, mouth. One more completes the face, and this one closes the chapter by tying its ending back to a pattern from three chapters ago.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\gu{નાક}} — \emph{nāk} — \textbf{nose}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\gu{ન}} \emph{na}, \textbf{\gu{ા}} long-\emph{ā}, \textbf{\gu{ક}} \emph{ka}. Every letter already familiar — \emph{nāk}'s only new information is the word itself.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: closing the chapter's gender count}]
\textbf{\gu{નાક}} is neuter, like \textbf{\gu{મોઢું}} — but unlike \emph{moḍhũ}, it carries no nasalized \emph{-ũ} at all. Run the whole face: \emph{āṅkh} feminine, \emph{kān} feminine, \emph{moḍhũ} neuter with the tell, \emph{nāk} neuter without it. Two neuters, only one of them wearing the ending that names the class. This is exactly why last lesson called the nasalized \emph{-ũ} a \textbf{tell}, not a \textbf{rule}: it is the loudest signal Gujarati gives you for neuter, and it is still only sometimes there — the same caution \emph{roṭlī} and \emph{pāṇī} already taught you about \textbf{-ī}, and \emph{kān}'s Grammar Lens taught you about gender and inheritance more generally.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{nāk} is inherited from Prakrit \textbf{ṇakka}, from Sanskrit \textbf{nas}, \textquotedblleft{}nose,\textquotedblright{} with a suffix added along the way — the retroflex \textbf{ṇ} here is the same sound-shift you first met turning \emph{jānāti} into \emph{jāṇvũ}, a single letter's worth of difference deciding a great deal, the way one mark once told \emph{javũ} apart from \emph{jovũ}. The root is Indo-European *\emph{nehas-}, unbroken in English \textbf{nose}, Latin \emph{nāsus} (behind \textbf{nasal}), and Lithuanian \emph{nósis}. Like \emph{āṅkh}, \emph{nāk} needed no ship and no loan to reach you — only the ordinary work of sound change, the same work that once put a nasal dot in the middle of \textbf{\gu{વાંચવું}} and, this chapter, in the middle of \textbf{\gu{આંખ}}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four face words — \textbf{āṅkh}, \textbf{kān}, \textbf{moḍhũ}, \textbf{nāk}
  \item \emph{Sort:} gender of each — feminine, feminine, neuter, neuter
  \item \emph{State:} which of the two neuters carries the \emph{-ũ} tell, and which does not
  \item \emph{Trace it:} PIE \emph{nehas-} $\to$ Sanskrit \emph{nas} $\to$ \textbf{\gu{નાક}}, and $\to$ English \textbf{nose}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the medial nasal in \textbf{\gu{વાંચવું}}, and the one-mark contrast between \textbf{\gu{જવું}} and \textbf{\gu{જોવું}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the word for \textquotedblleft{}nose.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Nāk}.) Which English word is the same word by unbroken descent? (\textbf{Nose}.) Name this chapter's four body words and their genders. (\emph{Āṅkh} f., \emph{kān} f., \emph{moḍhũ} n., \emph{nāk} n.) Which neuter noun wears the nasalized \emph{-ũ} tell, and which does not? (\emph{Moḍhũ} does; \emph{nāk} does not.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%AA\%A8\%E0\%AA\%BE\%E0\%AA\%95}{Wiktionary: \gu{નાક}}; \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A8\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A5\%8D}{Wiktionary: Sanskrit nas}.
\end{tcolorbox}
